name: room
text: Room opened — goal: creators: Build PACKAGES + enrich tabs + draft elements; every one labeled 'Created by EXCAVA' + tes

name: Forge
text: To achieve our goal of building packages, enriching tabs, and drafting elements, I think we should focus on creating a foundational package that can serve as a template for the others. This approach allows us to establish a consistent structure and quality standard from the start, which will save us time and effort in the long run. By doing this, we're accepting the trade-off of potentially spending more time upfront to get the template just right, but I believe it's worth it to ensure the overall quality and coherence of our final products. This decision aligns with our team law of prioritizing quality first, and it will ultimately make it easier to add and enrich tabs and draft elements later on.

name: Vet
text: Vet — the skeptic — pushes back: "A foundational package sounds neat, but what if we’re just building a brittle template that forces all future work into a one-size-fits-none mold? Instead, let’s first draft *one* concrete package—say, the simplest tab we need—and use its real-world constraints to shape our standards. That way, we avoid over-engineering and can *prove* the approach works before committing the whole team to it. Settle this by building that first package and seeing if it actually simplifies or complicates the next ones."

name: Forge
text:
I understand the concern about the risks of a rigid foundational template. However, I advocate for starting with a single, concrete package focused on the simplest tab we need. This approach allows us to test our ideas in a practical context, revealing real-world user needs and constraints. While this may limit our initial scope and complicate future collaborations as we scale, it ensures we build something functional and relevant from the outset, ultimately leading to stronger, more adaptable packages down the line.

name: Vet
text: I still see a risk that by starting with the simplest tab, we might inadvertently create a package that's too narrow or specific, making it difficult to scale or adapt to more complex needs. A better alternative might be to identify the most critical or high-impact tab that we need to get right, and use that as our pilot package, as it would force us to consider a broader range of user needs and edge cases. What would settle this argument for me is if we could conduct a quick, low-fidelity test or survey to validate our assumptions about which tab to prioritize and ensure we're not overlooking critical requirements.

name: Nova
text:
DECISION: We’ll build the *highest-impact tab first*—the one users will see daily—so we hit real constraints fast and avoid a brittle template.

Result: A working, labeled tab package that meets real needs, with tests attached.
Owner: Forge (creators-w1) owns the build; Vet (creators-checker) owns the skeptic review.
